summary: A Dublin feature dated September 14th 2023 on how Irish families keep customs alive across generations, through food, festivals, music, language, education, diaspora reunions and digital media. It profiles specific families in different Dublin neighborhoods, each embodying one tradition. It concludes that traditions survive by adapting while honoring the past.
one_line: Profiles of Dublin families showing how Irish customs in food, festivals, music, language, education and digital media are passed down and adapted.
key_facts: The article is datelined Dublin, September 14th 2023.
The O'Connor family has roots dating back to early 19th century Ireland; patriarch Patrick O'Connor is 78 and remembers his grandparents storytelling by the fire and making boxty on a griddle.
The O'Sullivan family of Rathmines prepares weekly Sunday dinners; Maeve O'Sullivan passes down recipes from the great famine.
Declan O'Sullivan, Maeve's grandson, is learning to make traditional soda bread from his grandmother.
The Healy family of Leeson Street observes Samhain, an ancient Gaelic festival marking the end of harvest, with extended family for reflection, storytelling and honoring ancestors.
The Kelly family of Temple Bar celebrates St. Patrick's Day by wearing heirloom Celtic jewelry, parading through Dublin's streets and publicly reciting Irish poetry and music.
The O'Neills of Ballsbridge hold weekly Saturday ceilidhs with fiddle and bodhran, and have adopted modern variations of traditional dance and tunes.
The Murphy family of Donnybrook speaks Gaeilge at home and supports local Gaeilgeoiri groups and Irish-language schools, insisting on bilingualism in education.
The Flynns of Clontarf champion including Irish history and customs in school curricula; their mother is a former history teacher.
The Moloneys, with relatives across America and Australia, hold an annual reunion on their forebears' departure anniversary, mixing in-person and virtual attendance.
Young members of the Keogh family use Instagram and YouTube to document gatherings, festive attire and traditional meals.
The article's closing section asks whether traditions will survive changing demographics, global influences and shifting values, answering that daily reaffirmation and adaptation are key.
